paragraphs: Here's what I want you to take from this one, friend. David's problems were real. Foes were rising up, and many were saying, "God will not deliver him" (Psalm 3:2). He didn't pretend the crowd wasn't there. He told the LORD all about it, out loud, and that's the first lesson: you can bring the whole mess to God.

Then comes the turn, and it changes everything. "But You, O LORD, are a shield around me, my glory, and the One who lifts my head" (Psalm 3:3). The crowd didn't get smaller, but David stopped staring at it and looked at the LORD. That's why he could say, "I lie down and sleep; I wake again, for the LORD sustains me" (Psalm 3:5). His rest came from who was holding him, not from how quiet things were. I slept fine in a junk drawer once I figured that out. Well, FINE. Dusty, but fine.

So when your own crowd shows up, baker, do what David did. Cry aloud, say the "But," and let the LORD be the shield. David even prayed hard and honest, asking God to save him and strike back at his enemies (Psalm 3:7), and he still ended where every prayer should land: "Salvation belongs to the LORD; may Your blessing be on Your people" (Psalm 3:8). The rescue was never his job. Your job is to bring it to the One whose job it is.
